speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: JAPAN-VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS ON EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the House I should like to table a copy of a letter dated June 25 from the Ambassador of Japan, informing me of the voluntary restraints which the Japanese Government is applying on the export of certain products to Canada during 1965.
These decisions were taken by the Japanese Government following consultations which began in December, 1964 between representatives of the Japanese and Canadian Governments. The levels of restraint which Japan is maintaining during 1965 provide generally for orderly increases over the 1964 levels. These increases, with but a few exceptions, are in the order of 3 to 5 per cent, and for virtually all products these increases are not greater than the expected growth in the market for the products in question.
With the approval of the House, I suggest that the Ambassador's letter be printed as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings.
I should like to inform hon. Members that I received representations from textile producers some time ago about the sharp and substantial increase within the cotton fabric quota in Japan's exports of converted broadcloth. The question has been raised with the Japanese Government and discussions on this matter are continuing.
I should also mention that representations were received from the textile industry about the impact of Japanese man-made fibre fabrics on the Canadian market. As a result of these representations we have drawn to the attention of the Japanese Government our concern about the way certain lines of manmade fabrics are being marketed, and we have asked that they examine this situation in order to ensure that a policy of orderly marketing is followed for these products.
As Members of the House may recall, a number of products have been freed from restraint during the last few years. This year, continuing this Government's policy of not asking for restraints when disruDtion to the 22620-1811
Canadian market is no longer threatened, we have agreed that five items should be freed from restraint. These are spun rayon blouses, spun rayon shirts, canvas footwear, waterproof footwear, and dish towels. I have no doubt that the Japanese Government will interpret this as concrete evidence of the willingness of the Canadian Government to work toward the orderly expansion of two way trade between our two countries.

speechtext:

However, it is instructive to see that the procedures which have been in use for some time are being continued, and that the aims of these procedures which were outlined by a former Minister of Finance, Mr. Fleming, are being achieved, notwithstanding that a goodly number of the Minister's colleagues were bitterly critical about such procedures when they were on this side of the House; and in this connection I am looking particularly at the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). I am very pleased to see that responsibility of office has rather matured the thinking of the present administration, if such a step is possible in certain sectors.
I hope Canadian industry, and generally the country at large, will understand the aims, certainly the impact, of quotas, even though these are not the same in various parts of the country, and one may hear some rather sharper comments from western Canada which, of course, has a different slant with regard to trade with Pacific nations than has the rest of the country.

I direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister. It concerns the issue or grant of an undersea exploration permit by the Federal Government in respect of areas adjacent to the Gaspe and the statement by Mr. Levesque that the grant constitutes a coffin nail for Confederation; also the criticism by the Premier of Quebec that what took place was most improper.
Has the Government given consideration to discontinuing the granting of permits of this kind, in view of the fact that it has sub-
June 25, 1965

mitted to the Supreme Court of Canada the British Columbia claim to such rights? I thought I would address this question to the Acting Prime Minister because this is a matter which covers several departments. I notice he indicates that he wants to hear from the Minister of Northern Affairs, but I am directing my question to him because of his all-pervasive and comprehensive knowledge of these matters. I ask him whether the Government will reconsider the undertaking given by the Prime Minister that this whole question should be considered at the Dominion-Provincial Conference to be convened in July rather than permitting it to become an interprovincial-Federal squabble which could certainly do nothing toward a solution of this problem and which might bring about further disunity within this country.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS ISSUE OF EXPLORATION PERMIT FOR GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think this matter comes within the purview of my hon. friend the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and he might care to make a reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS ISSUE OF EXPLORATION PERMIT FOR GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in anticipation of this question being asked today I have reviewed the facts. I would like to advise the House that Canada oil and gas permits have been issued for a period of years, under the Canada Oil and Gas Regulations, since the Convention on the Continental Shelf agreed to at the United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea in 1958 confirmed that rights to these submerged resources belong to Canada.
The Minister responsible should not and does not select on the basis of discretion which bona fide applicants are to receive grants of exploratory permits and which applicants are not allowed to obtain permits. Pan American Petroleum Corporation made regular application for exploratory permits in the Gulf of St. Lawrence on June 9, 1965. It is the view of the Federal Government that as the seabed resources of the Gulf of St. Lawrence do not lie within the boundaries of any province,
Inquiries of the Ministry they are subject to the administration of the Federal Government.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition raised the question of the reference to the Supreme Court of Canada in respect of the Province of British Columbia. The House is aware that this Government has referred the question of the jurisdiction over submerged resources on the Pacific coast to the Supreme Court of Canada. This action was taken because of the position of the Province of British Columbia that it held exclusive jurisdiction to control the exploitation of these off-shore resources, a position which the Federal Government does not accept. It was our hope that the issues raised by this first reference would give a clear indication of the respective rights of the Federal Government and the Provinces in this particular question.
I do not think I need to say any more at this time. We have been issuing these permits, on the basis of the Canada Oil and Gas Regulations, to bona fide applicants in the normal procedure and the normal way.

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I come back to the source of all information-I did not say of wisdom-and ask the Acting Prime Minister whether the Federal Government will carry out the promise it made that this question of underwater rights would be discussed at the Federal-Provincial Conference on July 19, rather than following the haphazard, uncertain course that is being followed now, to which the Minister has made reference. Is this dispute going to be settled, rather than through this course, through the instrumentality of that so-called new federalism that has brought about so much division?

However, this general question is on the agenda for discussion at the Federal-Provincial Conference and I would hope that as a result a solution satisfactory to all parties could be found.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ENQUIRY AS TO CANADIAN POSITION REGARDING DEFAULTING NATIONS
speechtext: I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether the Government of Canada has now reversed the stand it took earlier that defaulting members of the United Nations should, under the charter, be denied the right to vote. Has the Government altered its view in this regard, and does it now intend to support the action to assure that the U.S.S.R., France and other defaulting nations shall not be denied the exercise of their full rights under the charter by reason of their default?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ENQUIRY AS TO CANADIAN POSITION REGARDING DEFAULTING NATIONS
speechtext:
The Canadian Government, of course, has not changed its view about the application of Article 19 to a situation where a member is in default for an amount greater than its assessment for the two previous years. Earlier this year the Canadian Government made its stand known when Albania moved for the resumption of the normal business of the Assembly. We said we did not regard our vote on that occasion as in any way prejudicing the position which we felt should legally be taken with regard to Article 19.
But the Canadian Government now thinks, this question having been affected by the vote on that occasion, it would be regrettable

for the future integrity and usefulness of the United Nations if we were to have a repetition of the stalemate which attended the deliberations of the United Nations last December and January. The British Government, the Scandinavian Governments, New Zealand, Iceland and Canada have made voluntary payments toward the financial situation facing the United Nations. We hope this will help create a climate in which it will not be necessary for the Assembly to meet next September faced with the frustrating circumstances that attended the last Assembly. I think the wise course would be to seek to proceed with substantive business, and to regard the application of Article 19 as having been resolved for this situation alone along the lines of the statement made by Canada last February.

subtopic: ENQUIRY AS TO CANADIAN POSITION REGARDING DEFAULTING NATIONS
speechtext: In this situation it is difficult for me to follow exactly what the situation is, using the words of the hon. gentleman. Does this mean that Canada's position now is that regardless of the default on the part of the U.S.S.R., its puppet nations and France, when the session opens this fall Canada will give support to deliberations being continued and votes taken, regardless of whether contributions have been made by the defaulting nations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ENQUIRY AS TO CANADIAN POSITION REGARDING DEFAULTING NATIONS
speechtext: Yes, Sir.

In addition, I criticized the arm's length provision because it appeared to me there can be definite arm's length relationships even though persons may be related, within the same family.
I cannot see why such a limitation as this should be imposed. With regard to the proposed paragraph (aa) dealing with expenses, I believe the Minister has a laudable object in mind in dealing with legitimate expenditures, but I am wondering what yardstick of reasonableness is being used with regard to the interpretation of this paragraph. I suppose the same broad tests of reasonableness will apply to these expenses as to any other business expenses. I think it does raise this question, because the assessor must make up his mind whether any expense is a reasonable one to be charged against the business. In this particular case there is, of course, an added check. If a client retains a lawyer and the lawyer charges excessive fees, or his expenses are unreasonable in the opinion of the client, then perhaps

How can the officials of the Department of National Revenue actually establish that in the case of a private bill it was only necessary for one or two of the petitioners to come here accompanied by counsel, when it might have been just as reasonable for say five of the petitioners to come here?

the Royal Commission on Taxation last year by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Employees' Association on behalf of the employees of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool engaged in the construction and repair of country grain elevators, annexes and cottages, and made with the full knowledge and support of the employer, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool.

Apparently the complaint is that there is an anomaly in the Act with respect to the repair gangs that during the summer travel across the breadth and width of Saskatchewan to repair country elevators. The anomaly comes in because apparently the foreman of the gang who makes arrangements or contracts with the Wheat Pool, or any elevator company for that matter, for these repair jobs is exempt for income tax purposes with regard to food and other incidental expenses in the matter of travelling about the country, but the people he employs are not.
A foreman and any members of his gang are, in my estimation, in exactly the same capacity. This has been a complaint of long standing. There was a very lengthy submission made to the Royal Commission on Taxation on this matter, and I wonder whether the Minister has any observations to make in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is another of those difficult questions, Mr. Chairman. Expenses are allowed in the case of construction workers, and the fact that I think has got the Department into difficulty is that they are not allowed for some other kinds of workers. Not all the people my hon. friend has just mentioned come under the category of construction workers. I am not satisfied with the present divisions. I have not been able to come up with a clearcut answer that will be satisfactory in all cases. Again it is one of those things that I know is being studied by the Carter Commission. I do not know whether they have found a satisfactory answer. I hope their report will be available within a few months.

Mr. Chairman, might I suggest that the solution to this question would be just to include all members of these work gangs in the same category.

Mr. Chairman, unfortunately I was absent when the vote took place with reference to this clause, but I want to make clear the stand I took on behalf of this party, which was unanimously accepted. Clause 4 is one of the most serious potential invasions of freedom that this country has ever seen. I also want to emphasize that while the press generally places the responsibility in this regard on the Minister of Finance, this is a Government measure for which the Government must accept responsibility.
On the last occasion I spoke I made a plea for further consideration of this question, and that it be held back by the Government; and I am going to repeat it. Indeed, I will go further and state that apparently the Prime Minister of Canada, according to information I have secured from those who have been strong supporters of this Government, has
Income Tax Act
misled the representatives of the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association and given them an impression which is not borne out by the facts.
It is not the first time that we on this side of the House have seen under this Government deceptive and untrue statements made in the House of Commons, but this particular incident took place outside the House. I am going to refer to a statement made by the president of the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association which reveals a condition of affairs which cannot be condoned. In other words these representatives of the Association have been deceived, and deceived as the result of a statement made to them by the Prime Minister of Canada. I would say more were he present. I am going to refer to this statement because it shows an attitude of mind on the part of this Government that is not in keeping with parliamentary tradition or the ordinary principles that should prevail. On June 23 Mr. Graybiel said:
Last night-
That was the 22nd.
-I was asked to comment on the government's action in proceeding with press control legislation although the CDNPA had requested that such legislation be deferred until possible alternatives had been studied. My reply was "We are disappointed. We asked for time and we didn't get it".
I have been questioned as to why the CDNPA should expect the government to delay its legislative program.
He goes on:
On May 4, executives of the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association met Prime Minister Pearson and Finance Minister Walter Gordon-
The Minister was present, and he will get the opportunity to answer whether or not the statement of Mr. Graybiel represents the facts.
-to protest that the government's proposal was "a fundamental violation of long-established press freedom in Canada".
Following that meeting I wrote to Mr. Pearson: "You indicated to us yesterday your belief that there is some urgency in preventing foreign takeover of newspapers. Any immediate danger has, of course, been met by Mr. Gordon's announcement of the government's intention in his Budget address. No potential foreign investor will proceed with acquisition of a Canadian newspaper in the face of the government's stated intention to make advertising in such a newspaper taxable as of January 1, 1966. Presumably, that intention could be implemented by legislation at any time before the end of the year. Thus a breathing space of some eight months has been gained. That time can be devoted to exploration of alternative methods of achieving the government's objective.
That was a letter written to the Prime Minister setting out what had taken place.

June 25, 1965
Income Tax Act
What we are witnessing in the absence of the Prime Minister, who is in the United Kingdom, where he should be at this time, is that this legislation is being pushed through so the Government will be able to say "Well, really, the Prime Minister did not have an opportunity of making himself clear in this regard."
We want to know, Mr. Speaker, which newspapers are in danger of being taken over. The Minister of Finance has stated that the terrible danger of Canadian newspapers being taken over is imminent. While fearing for Canada's national identity, Time and Reader's Digest are placed in a position where they are set apart, given a kind of honorary Canadian citizenship wherein they are absolved from any of the dangers of which the Minister spoke. This legislation is just like bringing in law to prevent speeding on the highways because of the danger, and then restricting the law to those who go over 60 miles an hour. That is in reality what the situation is today, with $4 million of advertising going to these two companies.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
So far as Time magazine is concerned, one has only to read the Canadian edition week by week to realize the change in view in the last few months so obviously in favour of the Government. It has been very clear and very definite. No Liberal newspaper dedicated to Liberalism couid be so unobjective as Time magazine has been. Apparently this is the pay-off. I want to make it very clear that while it may be that this legislation is going to be put through, this is not going to be the last of the story. I read on:
Neither then nor since then did the Government question that assumption.
That is the assumption that nothing would be finally done for several months so as to enable the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association to make its representations and provide its alternatives.
On May 12 Mr. Pearson wrote me and, in fact, invited the publishers to suggest such alternatives.
The Prime Minister said this in his letter, as quoted by Mr. Graybiel:
"We will be more than glad to give further thought to any alternative which the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association would submit...I will be only too happy to give the fullest and most sympathetic consideration to any alternative method of expressing the same principles which your Association can recommend."
Mr. Graybiel goes on to say:
On May 14 I replied to the Prime Minister, accepting on behalf of the C.D.N.P.A., Mr. Pearson's request for alternative solutions.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
The following is in quotations:
"A meeting of the executive committee.. .has been called for June 15 to give further consideration to this matter. In the meantime I forwarded copies of your letter to each of the 104 members of the C.D.N.P A. requesting them to send me their comments and suggestions so that the executive committee may consider them."
Thus Mr. Pearson knew that the publishers were studying alternative proposals, knew that they believed they had eight months to achieve an effective alternative solution, knew that the next stage in the study was a meeting of the C.D.N.P.A. executive committee on June 15.
What a travesty of an agreement. The views of the C.D.N.P .A. conformed exactly with the views of the Prime Minister as set out in his letter. Mr. Graybiel went on to say:
In the face of that knowledge, the Government introduced its legislation in the House of Commons on June 14.
What is behind all this? Why this haste? Why not wait until the Prime Minister gets back so we can ask him, if we cannot get any information from the Minister of Finance, whether this is true? Mr. Graybiel goes on:
When I protested this hasty action, the officers of the C.D.N.P.A. were invited by the Acting Prime Minister, Hon. Paul Martin, to meet with him and Mr. Gordon in Ottawa on June 18. We pointed out that if the Government denied us the time to carry out the Prime Minister's invitation to supply alternatives, and proceeded with the legislation, the achievement of any alternative solution would be virtually impossible. The study which the C.D.N.P.A. had undertaken at the Prime Minister's request would be meaningless. Following this meeting the Government went ahead and the bill received second reading in the House last night.
Then he goes on to say:
I think this statement of facts makes it clear why the C.D.N.P.A. asked that action be deferred and why we were disappointed that our request was not granted. We were only trying to do what we had been invited to do by the Prime Minister and only requesting the time for our study which we had been led to believe was available to us.
That is the way the last line appears in the statement, but it has been suggested to my office that the last line should read "which we believed was available to us".
What is the rush? Are these newspaper proprietors parasites? Are they not Canadians entitled to the consideration which it was agreed should be given to them? Why this rush? What is going on? Who is going to benefit? What is behind this? Are certain American magazines forcing action at this session? Is that the reason? Is one of the reasons, if you do this we will do that? It is difficult to understand what is behind this.
I am not going to go over the facts I have dealt with on previous occasions, but over the

years I have never seen the Winnipeg Free Press, which has supported this Government, take such a stand. I do not want to see the Minister of Finance pilloried and placed in this disgraceful assortment of people whose pictures appear here. The whole Government should be there.
Yellow journalism.

There seems to be some confusion as to what the meaning of freedom of the press is. I have always taken it for granted that the freedom of the press involves the right of a Canadian citizen to publish news that is not obscene and that is not libelous, to publish opinions on public affairs that are not obscene and not libelous, and that it has nothing whatsoever to do with the question of the ownership of the means by which these views are disseminated.
We have before us a measure which does attempt to curb, shall we say, some of the business freedom of those who own the properties of mass communication. Nowhere that I can see is there any suggestion whatever that powers are being conferred upon the Minister of Finance, or any other dignitary, to dictate the editorial policies of any paper. But the Minister is taking steps to try-I think rather ineffectively-to prevent these organs of public opinion falling into the hands of non-Canadians and thereby being at their disposal to disseminate views, ideas and opinions that may not be in the best interests of Canada but may be in the interests of some other part of the world.
This does not seem to me to be any intrusion into the freedom of the press. It seems to me to be merely a wise precaution to make sure that if we are going to have opinions widely

disseminated, they will be disseminated by fellow Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before clause 4 is put to the vote I should like to reply very briefly to two points which were made by the Leader of the Opposition in his remarks. I say very briefly, because this matter was fully debated at the appropriate time when the bill was before the House on second reading.
The first point made by the Leader of the Opposition was in regard to Time and Reader's Digest. I sometimes wonder whether the right hon. gentleman's memory is as good as it should be. He was complaining about the exemption and yet, as I recall it, it was his Government which was the first to propose an exemption for Time and Reader's Digest. It was not exactly the same as the present exemption; nevertheless the principle was the same. He is now taking another tack. He is almost standing on his head, if I might put it that way. If I were tempted to ask the kind of rhetorical questions in which he sometimes indulges, I might ask him why this change of tune.
The point I wanted to make seriously- because while the other is serious we have covered it before-is in reply to the statement issued by Mr. Richard Graybiel, the president of the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association. Perhaps I might be
June 25, 1965

permitted to remark that Dick Graybiel is a very old personal friend of mine.
He was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are the kind of friends who remain friends despite honest differences of opinion about this or any other matter. I can say that on my part and I am equally sure I can say it on the part of Mr. Graybiel. It is a friendship which I happen to value very much.
The Leader of the Opposition, to my surprise, said that the Prime Minister had deceived-and he used the word "deceived"- the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association. If I may say this to him, I think he makes these loose charges too frequently. If there is any excuse for him on this particular occasion it may be in the wording of the last sentence of Mr. Graybiel's widely distributed statement, particularly in the last clause in that sentence. The sentence reads:

Mr. Graybiel is an honest and very fairminded man. During the course of the right hon. gentleman's remarks I received a telegram from Mr. Graybiel which I tried to get permission to read at the time and in the context of the other statement. us".

I regret very much the fact that the representatives of the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association went away with an impression which differed from mine. However, I hope I have cleared up this 22620-182

point or rather that Mr. Graybiel has cleared it up. There was certainly no deception. It was a misunderstanding which I am sure both sides will regret. Apart from that, Mr. Chairman, I do not think there is anything I need to add to what has been said.

Mr. Chairman, I want to point out immediately that when I read the Graybiel communication into the record I read it with the change in question. I said it has been altered. But, Mr. Chairman, there is no difference except in verbiage. The fact still remains that the whole body of the statement indicates that there was never a clearer revelation on the part of anyone as to the understanding which the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association had. The only deviation is in the last line and there is not very much difference between the two phrases. But I did use the altered form when I read the statement into the record.
When the hon. gentleman says that I am standing on my head I do not want to enter into competition with him. He has established a record in that regard that makes me quite concerned that he should ever suggest that I would be guilty of the same thing, because from the day he became Minister of Finance he has shown an aptitude in that connection that has never merited comparison in the House of Commons throughout the last 25 years. The only difference between those who do this as a profession is that they are actually on their heads while he is standing on his feet when he utters these views. But that is an aside.
The Minister says he cannot understand the change of front. There has been no change of front. We set up a Royal Commission for the purpose of looking into a cause of complaint, but not from the newspapers of Canada. The newspapers have never asked for this legislation. They do not want it. They are being forced into a strait-jacket by a Minister who along with the Government must have some reason for doing something which has not been requested by the newspapers across Canada with the exception of not more than one or two.
Why is this being done? The Minister says he explained it earlier. I have read every line of his explanation and at no time has he placed the reason before the House or the Canadian people. Strong representations were made by Maclean's magazine and by other Canadian magazines that it was impossible for them to compete against masquerading Canadian magazines whose material was

June 25, 1965
Income Tax Act
prepared outside the country and then brought into Canada. They asked for some measure of protection against an invasion that could not be justified, an invasion of those from another country who, pretending to be Canadian, are actually placed in a category that denies fair competition.
The O'Leary Commission said that action would have to be taken if we were to maintain a Canadian quality, a Canadian identity. Evidence was heard for a lengthy period of time and finally the recommendation was made that advertising in these magazines should not be credited in determining income tax by Canadian advertisers. That went a long way. We looked into the matter, discussed it from every angle and concluded that the only way to preserve Canadian magazines against this unjust competition would be to make changes in the credit, and I think the credit arrived at was to be 50 per cent.
What is being done now is to place these magazines on an equal basis with all Canadian magazines. Do not tell me that Time magazine looks at the Canadian scene as a Canadian magazine. All you have to do is to take the international edition of Time distributed round the world and see how often Canada is mentioned. I doubt that there has been more than a passing reference to Canada in the last 10 issues of international Time. Canada receives less attention than does a republic with 300,000 population. Yet Time is able to bring in all this material against which Canadian magazines cannot compete. In order to preserve the Canadian identity we took this course to protect Canadian magazines in Canada against an impossible situation.
But what is being done now? Time and Reader's Digest are being placed in the top category. They are being given honorary Canadian citizenship. They are being placed above all other magazines that may come into Canada. In addition, the newspapers of Canada are to be under the domination of a law that says you shall not dispose of your interest in any Canadian newspaper. Nobody asked for it. Why is it being done?
I conclude my remarks by saying that in a period of two years and two months we have had more fancy, socialistic tinkering going on on the part of the Government than any socialist government could ever have thought of, had it been in office.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to say a few words on this matter, partly because of the ruling you made with regard to the amendment proposed by the hon. Member
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. I do not want to be critical of the Chair because we on this side have found you, Mr. Chairman, to be eminently fair, and I am sure the ruling you made was made on the basis of your consideration of the rules as you understand them. But I want to say that I think your ruling was a very happy one for Members on the other side. Members like the hon. Member for York-Scarborough, the hon. Member for Carleton and the hon. Member for Northumberland like to consider themselves as being Liberals with a small "1". They will be very happy with the fact there is no need for them to put themselves on record in support of this fantastic and completely irresponsible recommendation made by the Minister of Finance. They are happy about that because nobody will be able to point to Hansard and say that on such and such a date these Members voted for making Time and Reader's Digest honourary Canadian citizens. Your ruling, therefore, was a very fortunate one for them.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
Some of us knew the Minister of Finance before he came to this House. It seems to me that when he was the president of the Canadian Institute for International Affairs and when he wrote that famous book which he probably wishes now he had never written, "Troubled Canada", when he expressed concern about keeping Canada for Canadians, while we may not have agreed with everything he said, he at least showed some concern with some of the major problems, and attempted to come up with some answers. What we have today, Mr. Chairman, I submit is a complete capitulation on the part of the Minister of Finance to the political needs and desires of the Liberal Party. How could anyone who has read the O'Leary Commission report possibly introduce this type of legislation to establish laws whereby Canadian publications will be owned and controlled by Canadians when, in fact, Time and Reader's Digest have taken over a major portion of the magazine industry in Canada? What the Minister is doing is locking the barn door after the horse has been stolen.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this may be fine for the Liberal Party which is great on words but so lacking in action, but it certainly is not going to satisfy anybody else. The Minister gets angry when we discuss this and I suppose he gets angry because he knows he is in such a weak position. The leader of this party tells a story about the sexton of the church who was cleaning up the church when

he found some notes left by the minister on the lectern. He saw that in the margin there was a notation: Raise your voice at this point because the argument is weak. This is exactly what the Minister is doing. He has no defence of his action on behalf of Time and Reader's Digest, so he thinks if he ignores the situation it will go away, that people will forget it. Perhaps the people will forget it, but I suggest the Minister will remember it for a long time because he knows what he is doing is wrong and indefensible.
I want to say that I never saw a person more uncomfortable than the Minister was the other night when the hon. Member for Port Arthur was analysing the Minister's position. The Minister knew in his heart that everything the hon. Member for Port Arthur was saying was true and correct.
Why did you not vote for him?
The hon. Member asks why we did not vote with him. The Government made sure we could not vote with him-
Oh, oh.

Hon. Members can say, "Oh, oh" all they wish. I have lots of time. I do not want to go home today or Monday. If hon. Members like the hon. Member for York-Scarborough, who say, "Oh, oh," want to get up and defend Time and Reader's Digest why do they not do so? They sit in the back row and yell, "Oh, oh". I can take all their "Oh, oh's"; I have lots of time. They just do not have the courage to put on the record how they feel about it. We have been sitting here patiently throughout this debate waiting for some of these so-called small "1" Liberals. They like to say to the people in the cities, do not vote for the N.D.P. because, after all, we are going to do all the things they are talking about. Where are these people? I would be glad to permit a question because every time the hon. Member asks a question he puts his foot in it.
I was just wondering if the hon. Member who was asking, where are they, could answer this question: Where is the tiger from Port Arthur?

speechtext: Order; may I remind hon. Members that we are on clause 4, I believe, of Bill No. C-118.

I do not mind being reminded that we are on clause 4, Mr. Chairman. I wish that when Members like the hon. Member for York-Scarborough get up and ask these inane, useless questions, you would remind them that we are on clause 4. Then, I would not have to try to answer his stupid questions.
Let us just put on the record what the O'Leary Commission said about Time and Reader's Digest. I must admit that I am not in this chamber all the time, but I have looked through Hansard very carefully to see if the Minister ever tried to give an explanation of what the situation is. The O'Leary Commission points out that between the years 1950 and 1959, the gross advertising revenue of Reader's Digest went up from $1.5 million to $4.5 million, an increase of 194.1 per cent. The advertising revenue of Time magazine went up from just over a million dollars to over $3.5 million, an increase of 207.7 per cent. The gross advertising income of Canadian magazines went up just 57 per cent in this period.
Where is your spirit of competition?

The hon. Member asks,
where is my spirit of competition? It is not competition when a magazine like Maclean's has to pay for the writing and editing of every word which appears in the magazine, while Time magazine is only paying for the editing of four pages of that magazine. I am glad I am not a Liberal because if there ever was a failure to appreciate support which has been given, it is found in the Liberal Party. If there ever was a magazine which was more strongly Liberal than Maclean's, I do not know of it. I like Blair Fraser, but if Maclean's magazine pays him, then they are foolish because the Liberal Federation ought to pay him his whole salary. I have never seen him write anything critical of the Liberal Party.
However, that does not enter into this matter, the policy of the magazine. What concerns us as backbenchers is to find out how a magazine like Time can get to the Minister of Finance. If they cannot, then, as they could not last year, they get to the Prime

Two "Canadian" editions, Time and Reader's Digest have been getting over 40 per cent of the total spent on magazines in Canada...
In the case of Time, this consists of its taking the bulk of the Time (U.S.) editorial content and prefacing it with four pages on Canadian affairs.
I should like to interject that one might at least expect that for the privilege of making the millions they do in Canada they would run those four pages, biased as they generally are and pro Liberal as they usually are, in their United States edition so their United States readers might know something about Canada. They would not learn much, reading Time.

Reader's Digest draws exclusively from the central editorial pool created by the United States edition, but employs an editorial staff in Canada to provide boxes and footnotes, explaining the Canadian aspects of the editorial material obtained from this central pool.

The actual cost of obtaining and preparing the editorial material made available to these 'Canadian' editions is far beyond what they or Canadian magazines could possibly afford-

-bearing in mind the size of the Canadian magazine-reading population. The argument is clear and so unanswerable that the Minister of Finance and the

One can only conclude from reading the debate and looking at the legislation that this measure is deliberately designed to let those two publications remain in Canada, and to be classified as Canadian which, I suggest, is completely unprincipled and dishonest.
Some days ago the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond asked whether these so-called Canadian organizations are prohibited from buying and operating radio and T.V. stations, and the Minister answered that they are. But for him to say they are is not good enough. We would like to know how they are prohibited from owning radio and T.V. stations. What clause in the legislation prohibits them?
Suppose Mr. Luce or the owners of Reader's Digest decided they would like to buy into a Canadian daily newspaper, what part of this legislation will prohibit them from doing that? Like so much other legislation proclaimed by the Liberal Party before attaining office as designed to help to meet the needs of the Canadian people this, when it is analysed, demonstrates it will do little if anything.
Speaking of the newspapers, I suppose no government has had such unanimous opposition to any proposal at any time as this Government has had with respect to its proposal regarding the newspapers. I usually find myself disagreeing with the editorial positions of Canadian newspapers, and there is not a newspaper which I disagree with as often as the Winnipeg Free Press, in my own city. However, the Minister should have agreed to stand this part of the measure until the newspapers had an opportunity to make proposals to him for alternative means of ensuring that Canadian newspapers will not be owned by foreign interests.
I agree with the principle that Canadian newspapers should not have foreign owners. We have not had difficulty in that respect in Canada as yet, but anyone who has read the history of Europe will remember that before World War II many French newspapers were owned or subsidized by foreign groups from Nazi Germany, and they were very, to say the least, chary of being critical of Hitler.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. Member for Perth has posed an interesting and unusual problem. I understand his question concerns a person who goes outside Canada and wants to maintain a niece or nephew outside Canada at the same time. It is my understanding that this clause does not provide relief in the circumstances cited.

A niece or nephew is supposed to be in the same category as a dependant child, but in this instance that is not going to be so. Is this not right?
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)

I am wondering whether we could not clarify this by reference to clause 6(2) where the wording may be more felicitous. Paragraph (da) says the aunt or uncle of the taxpayer must be resident in Canada. That is the test. Nothing is said about the taxpayer's residence, and this is the point the hon. Member for Perth has in mind. The residence in the case of the nephew or niece need not be that of the taxpayer. The person who is posted abroad is deemed to be a resident of Canada. I think the true intent of the clause is to refer to the niece or nephew rather than to the taxpayer or his spouse,
although the language is not as felicitous as that used in paragraph (da)-
-was the aunt or uncle of the taxpayer or his spouse and was
(i)	resident in Canada, and
(ii)	dependant upon the taxpayer for support by reason of mental or physical infirmity.
I would say that in the case of a nephew or niece the test should be that of the nephew or niece being resident in Canada rather than the taxpayer or his spouse. After all, as the hon. Member for Perth indicated, this is to place a nephew or a niece in the same category to all intents and purposes as a dependant child, and surely it is the dependant child who must be resident in Canada, though in the case of ambassadors and so forth the children may be with them and deemed to be fully resident. In this case I suggest the test should be the residence of the nephew or niece as clearly indicated in respect to the aunt or uncle.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I believe my answer to the question asked by the hon. Member for Perth carried that inference. I said I doubted whether a nephew or niece outside Canada could claim. I think it does, except for this one distinction, the distinction raised by the hon. Member in his question.
Does not the Parliamentary Secretary feel that this distinction is one which should be removed?

speechtext: I would draw the hon. $500 in the case of a taxpayer who, before the end of the year, has attained the age of 65 years but has not attained the age of 70 years, if no pension under the Old Age Security Act has been authorized to be paid to him for any month in the year.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about the part of this clause that takes away the $500 exemption in certain instances for persons between the ages of 65 and 70. The hon. Member for Perth has already pointed out a particular unfairness, namely the case of one who turns 69 in November of next year and therefore gets only one month of the pension and loses the $500 exemption; but I should like to press the point that there is an even more fundamental unfairness in this arrangement. I do so by asking the Minister to anticipate the time when old age security will be generally available at age 65. When that time comes there will be thousands of Canadians drawing old age security-indeed, all Canadians who have the residence qualification and are 65 years of age or over. Those between 65 and 70, if they are single, will be entitled to only $1,000 income tax exemption, whereas those who are 70 and over will be entitled to $1,500 income tax exemption.
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I think this is unfair and that the Minister, instead of moving in the direction of taking away this extra $500 exemption from some people, should have moved in the direction of extending it across the board. The minute I say that, Mr. Chairman, there is brought to mind the two arguments that the Minister of Finance used with respect to the amendment that was moved some time ago by my colleague the hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. He moved, as the Minister will recall, that there be no tax payable by single persons earning less than $1,500 or by married persons earning less than $3,000. At first there was a misinterpretation of that amendment by the Parliamentary Secretary, who thought this was raising the $500 exemption generally and that it would produce huge reductions in taxation in the upper income brackets. When we straightened the Government out on that point, the Minister of Finance then saw the difficulty of people earning just over $1,500 as compared with people earning just under $1,500.
Surely there is another way to do it. Surely one does not solve this problem only by
June 25, 1965

raising the exemption levels to $1,500 and $3,000 for everybody, giving the greatest bonanza to the Gordon Sinclairs and those people who are propagandizing this idea in its simplest form. Surely you do not have just to run into a notch problem. Surely it is possible to start a new schedule of rates, to start at $1,500 for a single person and $3,000 for a married person and change the rates so that those in the lower and middle income brackets save a little, or at least do not pay any more income tax, but those in the upper income brackets do not get any reduction. Surely, Mr. Chairman, that is the kind of thing that ought to be done with the money the Minister has to apply to this purpose.
I realize that in effect I am speaking both to the question of withdrawing the $500 exemption for people between age 65 and 70 and the proposal that comes later to give a 10 per cent reduction in income tax itself. Surely the better way to have solved this problem would have been to raise the income tax exemption levels to figures like $1,500 and $3,000 and then to adjust all the rates right from the first $1,000 of taxable income up, so that the desired objective would be achieved. Surely the desired objective is to lessen the burden on those in the lower and middle income brackets without any necessity of lowering the burden on those in the upper income brackets. I mentioned our mutual friend Gordon Sinclair a minute ago because the Minister of Finance mentioned correspondence he has had with him. I had the experience of meeting this gentleman a few weeks ago on a television program and I found that he was particularly concerned, at least he seemed to be, in raising the income tax exemption level; but when I suggested that along with that there should be an adjustment of rates so that wealthy people- and I thought Mr. Sinclair might be one of them-would not get a terrific advantage at the top, I found that the interest was not quite as keen.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, there are not just one or two ways to do this. There are various ways. The income tax people over the years have been able to change the schedules, to change the rates, to change the progression. Surely the time has come to recognize that $1,000 and $2,000 are not sufficient exemption levels in the light of today's cost of living and today's standard of living. Surely common sense calls for higher exemption levels. We have been saying for a long time that the exemptions should be set at $1,500 and $3,000.
Income Tax Act
If we do not win this point soon, we are going to have to start asking for higher levels, perhaps $2,000 and $4,000. But surely we do not balk at this and do nothing about it because it creates problems at either end of the scale. The job, surely, is to decide what is a proper exemption level and then to adjust the percentage rates so that you collect a fair amount of tax, but not too much, from those in the lower and middle income brackets and collect what they can afford to pay from those in the upper income brackets.
I am glad the Minister is back in the chamber. When I was getting to my feet I was going to say that the Minister had the right to go out and have his lunch and I would have to keep talking until he got back; but he has had his lunch and is back in the chamber. I would like to hear what his thinking is on this question and what led him to take away this $500 exemption from people between age 65 and 70, instead of extending it across the board. Also, could he tell us now that the Government will consider, if not this year then certainly next year, doing this in a better way by raising the income tax exemption levels and changing the rates accordingly.

It has been my feeling right from 1948, I believe it was, when this provision was first introduced, that the Government has been too narrow as to what it allows as trade union dues. This clause takes into account the change in respect of corporations who have some interest in the business of oil, gas and mining. I do not know whether there has been a practice that has been found to be improper by exploratory and development syndicates and their relationship between parent companies with regard to oil and gas rights, but apparently there is a suggested loophole in the operation of the Act since the amendments back in 1962 or 1963. It seems to me that it is under these amendments that the Minister proposes to close the loophole. I should like to have clearly enunciated by the Minister the type of loophole he is trying to close and why the present provision must come into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, the loophole applies in a case where an oil or gas right can be acquired by a joint exploration corporation, but its cost can be divided by its parent corporations. A joint exploration corporation is a special kind of company defined in section 83 (a), (d) and (e), which was passed in 1962. It is a company whose principal business is the production or marketing of petroleum products or natural gas, or exploring or drilling for petroleum or natural gas, or mining or exploring for minerals. Such a company must not have more than ten shareholders and those may be companies that are in the oil, gas or mining business. These shareholder companies provide the joint exploration company with the funds to carry out the exploration. The joint exploration company may then divide these exploration expenses amongst its shareholder companies. The joint exploration company renounces its right to deduct the exploration expenses it has incurred and each of its shareholder companies acquires the right to deduct its share of these expenses.
It has become apparent that the joint exploration rules can be used as a loophole if an oil company wishes to dispose of its oil and gas properties and not bring the proceeds into income as required by section 83(a). The method is that a subsidiary is set up to qualify as a joint exploration corporation, even if the parent is the sole shareholder. The properties or rights are sold to the joint exploration corporation, and the cost which 22620-1831
Income Tax Act
by definition is an exploration expense, is then renounced back to the parent for such amount to be included in its income. It seems that the joint exploration corporation can then be sold by the parent, if a buyer can be found who is not interested in obtaining a deduction for the cost of the property it has acquired.
The same general procedure can be used to divide corporations and maximize the 33J per cent depletion allowance. Production properties can be transferred to the subsidiary and the net operating profits would enjoy full depletion without being reduced by the parent company's exploration expenses, including the cost of the properties transferred.

There is one question that comes to mind as a result of the Minister's explanation. How is it that a joint exploration subsidiary or company is allowed to have only one corporate shareholder? I believe this is where the mistake arises. There is no such thing as a joint exploratory corporation if there is only one shareholder. The definition, by itself, immediately knocks it out.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak very briefly on third reading, but also to move an amendment. The purpose of my moving an amendment at this time is to try to get a vote of the House on a specific issue. At least we should like to get as close to that specific issue as we possibly can.
As all hon. Members are aware, we have found it rather preposterous that this assembly of grown men and women has not found a way in which to register its opinion on the proposal of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to exempt certain publications from a rule which he has brought in, as set out in clause 4 of the bill. There have already been two or three votes which have been interpreted in different ways by different media. It is understandable that there has been this mininterpretation, because when a vote is taken on a rather large package it is hard to say whether a favourable

vote is either for or against the items in the package that one may not like.
A good deal of the debate on the budget resolutions and on the Income Tax Act amending bill has centred around the Minister's proposals regarding foreign-owned periodicals and the foreign ownership of newspapers. We in this party agree with the attempt of the Minister to prevent the foreign takeover of newspapers. Perhaps "prevent" is not the word because the legislation does not prevent it but merely discourages it. We also agree with the general rule that he has proposed regarding foreign-owned periodicals. The one point where we think that the Minister is being inconsistent is in the special exemptions that he makes for certain periodicals. Those exemptions are spelled out in subsection (2) of the proposed section 12A of the Income Tax Act, which is to be found in clause 4 of the bill now before us.
At the resolution stage we tried to get a vote on this specific point but were unable to do so. On second reading we had hoped we would get a chance to vote on this specific point but it was not possible. We tried again today when we were in committee of the whole on clause 4 of the bill but again it was not possible. But we think it is now possible, least if we state our case clearly, to have a vote of the House on this specific issue.
One right that is enshrined in the rules is the right on third reading to move that a bill be referred back to Committee of the Whole. In years gone by there used to be amendments that included rather specific instructions as to what should take place in the Committee of the Whole, but the tendency in recent years on the part of the Chair has been to find fault with amendments that included instructions. However, even in recent years, in fact in this Parliament, amendments that merely sought a reference back for the consideration of a particular clause have been allowed.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in order to have an amendment placed before the House which will be in order, we have drafted an amendment in precisely the terms of amendments which have been allowed in this Parliament. Accordingly, I move, seconded by the hon. Member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Barnett):
That Bill No. C-118 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of reconsidering clause 4 thereof.

Carried.

speechtext:
Hon. Roger Teillet (Minister of Veterans
Affairs) moved the second reading of Bill No. C-126, to amend the Army Benevolent Fund Act.
He said: I must correct certain of the information I gave to the hon. Member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) the other day in answering a question as to rates of interest. Reading the statement I had in front of me, I skipped a line and told him the rate was now 3 per cent. The actual figure will emerge from the brief statement I now wish to make.
The Fund was established by the Army Benevolent Fund Act in 1947. The original net worth of the fund was $9,293,477. The original interest rate was 2| per cent. The plan for the fund was that there would be prospective beneficiaries for 50 years and that payments for the first 30 years would average $473,000 a year, with much smaller payments during the remaining 20 years. During the last ten years disbursements have averaged approximately $520,000 a year. The net disbursement in the fiscal year 1964-65 was $451,544.
The Act was amended in 1952 to increase the annual interest rate to 3i per cent on the first $5 million, and 2| per cent on the excess. In 1961 interest rates were again increased to 4 per cent on the first $5 million and 3 per cent on the excess. These rates are still in effect.
The fund has decreased more rapidly than was originally intended and on March 31, 1965 it amounted to $5,552,078. During the fiscal year 1964-65 the fund assisted in 3,085 cases. Because it is considered important that the fund continue to operate in accordance with the original plan, and because interest rates have tended to increase, the bill proposes a rate of 4| per cent per annum for a period of five years, and provides for further quinquennial adjustments in the rate by the Governor in Council. This proposal will result in increased interest payments of approximately $34,000 a year during the first five year period.

that the House go into Committee to consider the following resolution:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
As hon. Members know, the proposed resolution to amend the Judges Act will provide compensation for two additional High Court judges in Ontario and one additional judge of the County Court of Ontario-in this case a third County Court judge for Middlesex County-and one additional judge for the Supreme Court of New Brunswick.
The appropriate legislation has already been passed by the provincial legislatures. The Ontario Legislature has acted to provide for the expansion of their courts to accommodate the required number of judges by an amendment to the Judicature Act which received Royal Assent on April 14, 1965 and by the
[Mr. Herridge.)
County Judges Amendment Act which received Royal Assent on April 2, 1965. The Judicature Act of New Brunswick has been amended by the Legislature of New Brunswick, which amendment received Royal Assent on April 3, 1965.
In all cases the necessity for additional judges has been created by the heavy volume of litigation at the Supreme Court level which is perhaps the product of the affluent society in those two provinces. I have been supplied with some figures which indicate the extent to which litigation has grown in recent years. In Ontario there was a notable increase between 1953 and 1965. In 1953 there were 9,929 writs issued and in 1965 there were 18,546 writs issued, an increase of 87 per cent. Of cases set down for trial, in 1953 there were 4,407. This had increased in 1965 to 7,134, an increase of 52 per cent.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

I regret that I cannot answer the right hon. gentleman in that respect, Mr. Chairman. A more detailed comparison of the figures might be of some assistance. In regard to litigation in the City of Toronto, in January, 1965, of cases set down for trial in the non-jury, defended category there were 374. By 1965 in this category the number of cases had risen to 1,142, an increase of 205 per cent. Of nonjury, undefended cases, in 1955 there were 512 and in 1965 this had increased to 1,011, an increase of 97 per cent. Of jury cases there were 154 in 1955 and 660 in 1965, an increase of 329 per cent.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that the present Chief Justice of the High Court of Ontario is actively engaged in trying to reduce the list of cases outstanding, and the Registrar of that court, who has had very considerable experience in litigation, has said that the past eight months have been perhaps the busiest in the history of that particular court. The figures for the period January 1, 1965, to May 31 of this year indicate some improvement in
June 25, 1965

this regard. For example, the number of divorce cases disposed of in this period exceeds by 122 those set down for trial. In the same way, the number of jury cases disposed of in this five-month period from January 1, 1965, show that there were 880 cases set down for trial, and at the present time there are 632 outstanding, indicating a net disposal of 248 cases.
The figures do, however, indicate both a continuous increase in litigation and a considerable number of cases outstanding. In Toronto and Ottawa in the Province of Ontario, for example, there has been an expansion of actual courtroom facilities. In the City of Ottawa there is now room for two High Court judges to be sitting in Assizes at the same time. It is to meet the requirement for additional judges that these amendments are being put before the House.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. gentleman give us the figures as to the number of trial judges of the High Court of Ontario in 1955 and today. We had an example some years ago in the Exchequer Court where judgments were delayed so long that only the litigants had not forgotten that they had a case. Mr. Chairman, I have no record with regard to the second question. I think the general opinion of the profession, which is perhaps the best measure I can give, is that on the whole the High Court of Ontario does have a very good record of disposing of matters, once they are brought to trial. There may be individual instances where judgments have been long delayed, but on the whole I think it has moved along quickly.
With regard to the first question, the right hon. gentleman inquired as to the number of judges as between 1955 and 1965. In 1955 there were the Chief Justice of the High Court and 18 trial judges. At the present time there are the Chief Justice, of course, and 22 High Court judges. If this amendment passes the House there will be 24 judges at the trial level in addition to the Chief Justice.

speechtext:
There is just one other question I want to ask, Mr. Chairman. Per-
Judges Act
sonally I think it is very necessary that the courts be able to carry out their responsibilities expeditiously. There are some parts of our country where judges are not overworked in certain divisions, but in the High Court of Justice, having regard to the great increase in litigation which in large measure I think would be damage litigation arising out of automobile accidents, there has been made necessary a substantial increase in the number of judges.
While normally I thoroughly disagree with the situation whereby a Parliamentary Secretary, however qualified and able the particular hon. gentleman may be, introduces a resolution in the absence of the Minister, in this case on a Friday afternoon and being in a benevolent mood I am not going to raise this objection. But there is one other question that occurs to me. We want to be assured that our judiciary shall continue to be above reproach. They will not always be right, otherwise there would not be courts of appeal. But they have to be men of honesty, integrity and ability. Sir John A. Macdonald once said, when asked what the qualifications of a judge were in his opinion, "A man who is honest and willing to work, and if he knows a little law that would be no particular detriment". This is true. So often outstanding counsel are appointed to the bench and do not make the judges that others with less forensic experience make. However, in the field of honesty and integrity of judges we Canadians have been unusually fortunate. There has been one blot on the record in the last year or so, but that judge's conviction is still before the courts and therefore I will make no reference to it. However, there is a case in the Province of Ontario that I think deserves a full explanation by the Department of Justice. I mentioned the case of the High Court Judge who was convicted and sentenced to two years imprisonment and whose appeal is pending. I say no more about that. The very fact that there are so few of these cases causes wider publicity being given to those that do occur than would otherwise be the case. We not only expect honesty and integrity in the judiciary but we also have the right to expect, and demand, that judges shall not only be honest but shall have the appearance of being honest.
There is a case that has been before the courts. The judge in question was acquitted after preliminary hearing. I refer to Mr. Justice Landreville. I would like to know what is being done in connection with this

June 25. 1965
Judges Act
case. We have tried to get information but it has not been vouchsafed us. I am in no way judging the merits of the case; I am simply pointing out that what was revealed in the press does not contribute to that feeling of certainty with regard to the judiciary that we, in the British tradition, have a right to insist upon. I would like to know whether the judge has been asked to resign and what his reaction has been to any such suggestions that have been made.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
If he has refused to do that which I think, in the interests of justice, he ought to do, then what action is going to be taken by way of setting up a Commission to look into the case and make a recommendation to the Minister of Justice? I am being very restrained in the expression of my viewpoint, but certainly with that shadow which is cast over the Justice, litigants appearing before him would not be subject to too great criticism if they were to conclude that they would sooner be tried by another judge.

That, Mr. Chairman, indicates that the Department of Justice, which of course at the moment is not an issue before the House, must assure that justice is done.

I am referring to the case of a judge of the High Court of Ontario, a court which, according to the Minister, is overworked. I was wondering whether or not in addition to these two judges to the court there should be a third vacancy as well.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, along that same line of principle my point is this. How is it that a Supreme Court judge, who can only be appointed by the Government of Canada can be sentenced to two years for perjury, who appeals, and although he is not serving as a judge is paid his salary by the Government of Canada? To me that is an extraordinary situation. If a man is guilty of perjury, then by all means let him appeal. But why a man who is a judge should be paid by Parliament is, to me, a most ridiculous situation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: It is a shocking thing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, not being a lawyer I show some reluctance to get into this particular debate. However, I think justice affects not only the lawyers either in Parliament or the country but also those who are considered to be in court the peers of either the jurors or those persons who are accused. I endorse the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition in relation to Mr. Justice Landreville, and may I say I come from northern Ontario, where this judge lives. This matter is a disgrace. It is one which would not be allowed in any other calling, and would not have been allowed here had this man not been a judge. It is all very well to refer the case to the Bar Association, who themselves have said that this man should be removed from the bench; but I think it is a disgrace to ask anybody to go before this judge to obtain justice in view of the indication that his own hands may not be clean and that he may have abused the highest trust given to him by the people of Sudbury, who elected him to serve them in another matter.
I fail to see why this man has not been removed by the Government, and I think this failure raises with the layman a number of questions. The first question flows from the fact, as the Leader of the Opposition has just said, that the appointment of a judge may call for a man who has worked either in the legal field or other fields. It is not absolutely necessary that you have legal training to be a good judge, but-

What?
