subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: Well, I hope I have not misinterpreted him, though I may have done.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext: I never made that suggestion.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
I assumed that what he was saying was that you do not need legal training. I do not know whether this is true or not, but I think it is.
To make my point quite clear, there was recently appointed to the Supreme Court of Ontario a man I have had the privilege of knowing for many years, a lawyer in the Town of Timmins, Gregg Evans. This gentleman prior to his appointment did not go through the process of being Crown Attorney, nor did he go through any of the lower courts such as the Magistrate's Court or County Court. But I am sure that Gregg Evans will be one of the best Supreme Court judges that we have in Ontario, and I predict that he will have a long and illustrious future in this field. I say that because I know that as an individual he is a very honest, temperate and very fair man. For this reason Gregg Evans will make an excellent judge even though he has not been through some of the other avenues.
As I say, I was of the opinion that people who were not lawyers could be appointed judges, although I may not be correct about that. But let us make no mistake about it- political appointments are the usual type of appointments which are made. They have been made on many occasions. The one just mentioned was, I think, an occasion when a party needed a seat and a man was promoted to the bench to make room for another candidate. I can see the present holder of the seat for that particular riding being reluctant to do something about the situation in the province, for the very simple reason that a contribution was made in the political sense which, to some extent at least, warrants a certain amount of sympathy from those who had the benefit of the change of seat.
I think that the situation involving Judge Landreville is a disgrace of justice in the Province of Ontario. I believe that the Department of Justice must exercise some jurisdiction in this field. Even the Bar Association are now reluctant to have this judge try cases. I know of several other judges in other areas who are not considered acceptable. I know of one magistrate in Timmins who is not acceptable to me because I know of his prejudice; and certainly I would not accept him as a trial judge if I were charged with an offence before him. I think I could legiti-
Judges Act
mately make a very good case as to why he should not sit on my case.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
This matter affects a large number of people. It is the Government that really is responsible in this field and I do not think they have discharged their responsibility, although I may not fully understand the division of responsibility between the province and the federal Government with regard to who has supervision of the judges, and some of the other factors involved.
The Parliamentary Secretary referred to the delay in justice. This is something that is very apparent, of course, to everyone. I understood him to say that there is a backlog of 660 cases in Ontario. I wonder who is responsible for directing cases to the different judges? On a number of occasions I have been in lawyers' offices when they have been trying to find a judge to sit and hear a particular case, and have had great difficulty in doing so. This is particularly true in the months of July and August when all the judges want to go on holidays. It is true they are not considered to be the peers of average persons, but it seems odd to me that a judge should take a couple of months off in the summer while he makes up his mind whether he wants to hear a case and when he wants to hear it. It would appear to me that if the Bar Association in the province is going to be the disciplinary body, they are going to have to make a decision with regard to what outside work judges can take, because the taking of such work often results in delaying regular court cases.
I should like to hear the Parliamentary Secretary explain to us what results have flowed from the discussion we had a year or two ago. At that time I believe everyone was of the opinion that while outside work could be very lucrative to judges, it was not going to be necessary for them to do such work because we had increased the salaries of the judges considerably. I know that at that time it was left to the discretion of the judges to decide whether or not they would take outside work and whether or not it would interfere with their regular duties, but from my slight knowledge I know that the judge still controls whether or not he will sit on a case and when he wants to sit. It is the judge who makes this decision. Quite often it is unfair that a person involved in litigation should chastise his lawyer for not making proper arrangements and speeding up the hearing of the case when the fact of the

June 25, 1965
Judges Act
matter is he cannot find a judge to hear it, and is having difficulty in bringing the case before the courts. I think the House should have some explanation of how far we got in asking the judges to co-operate and discipline themselves in return for the large increase in their indemnity provided by Parliament.
The fact that there is a backlog of 660 cases warrants in my opinion not only the appointment of two new judges but action by the House in the very near future to try to get rid of the backlog of cases. If the two new judges are energetic young fellows and do not do anything else, it is quite possible that in one year they could handle the 660 cases. However, some of these cases may very well be very heavy because, as the Leader of the Opposition mentioned, they fall in the field of civil litigation and require the production of a great deal of evidence. This is a very time consuming thing and I would think that these two judges are not really going to solve the problem of the backlog of 660 cases in Ontario. I think it would be much better if we could get all of the other 22 judges to take their fair share of the load.
If the Parliamentary Secretary would indicate to us the case load of each of these 22 judges I predict that we would find a great disparity. Some judges work and some do not do a darn thing. I would be interested in knowing, for instance, how many cases Mr. Justice Landreville has dealt with in the past year. I should like to know how many cases there were in which those involved did not want to go before this judge, who has been morally found guilty of an offence. If it had been anyone else except a judge that person would have found himself paying the penalty that the president of the company involved paid. They were both accused of exactly the same thing, one on one side of the fence and the other on the other, but the man who offered the bribe received a sentence and the one who accepted it did not. To me this is discriminatory.
I like the phrase lawyers use that justice delayed is justice denied. I know of cases involving the unsatisfied judgment fund, which I presume fall largely within the jurisdiction of the County Court judges in Ontario, that have been in process for three to four years. People are screaming blue murder because they have not got a motorcar. There is no way they can get the kind of transportation allowance that would be allowed in other types of cases, and so the penalty being paid by these people is very great. Their situation has been vastly aggravated

by the fact they have not been able to get their cases before the courts.
I would have much preferred it if the Minister of Justice had been interested enough to be here this afternoon to pilot this measure through the House. I think the Parliamentary Secretary will agree with most of what I say because he comes from Ontario, but the Minister of Justice may not be aware of some of the factors involved in the administration of justice in that province, although the Province of Quebec may have different problems. I believe the Minister should be prepared to come before us and tell us the recommendations that have been made by the Province of Ontario, who these two judges are going to be and what qualifications they have. This might at least be of interest to us.
I should like the Government to be prepared to come before Parliament before long and indicate that some thinking has been done with regard to the appointment of judges and the loads they carry. Although I am not prepared to document it, I believe there is a great disparity between the work done by some judges and the work done by others. I say this because for some time I had considerable experience with Ontario judges in relation to arbitration and conciliation boards. We found there were certain judges who were always available, and quite often they were the ones we did not want. There were others we wanted and who were much more acceptable to us but they were involved in handling other legal matters. I could name some of them but I will not do so.
I can remember one who had a little English car and who came to Timmins one time. He charged us something over $200 for transportation, but if he put $5 worth of gas in that car to get to Timmins I would be very surprised. We paid the amount under protest, but when he charged the company involved in this particular case the same amount he had charged us they said it was an unreasonable charge, refused to pay and took him to the Bar Association. That is an aside.
The point I want to make is that the Minister of Justice must be aware of the disparity in work loads. I think we should find some way of distributing the loads much more evenly, and we must also find a better way of choosing new judges. The judges are supposed to discipline themselves. So are Members of Parliament. If you look around you can see those who are always here and those who are never here. We are supposed to discipline ourselves too, but this does not always work.

Well, you can look around and see the empty seats. I say the case loads are not being evenly distributed and that there is no discipline in this regard. I know personally that some judges in the Province of Ontario are greatly overworked. They are handling cases because someone asks them to do so and they know full well that they have more work than they should be undertaking. At the same time there are other judges who are carrying very little of the load.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I am quite pleased that we are adding two new judges but I would be much more pleased if I knew who they were going to be. I would also be much more pleased if there was an obligation on the Chief Justice of Ontario to come before a committee of the Justice Department and indicate which judges he wanted removed because they were not doing any work. I should like the Chief Justice to exercise some authority and report to the Government on this aspect of the matter. The lawyers are going to laugh and say it cannot be done, that it has never been done. I think it is a disgrace, and every person in Ontario will think it is a disgrace that Judge Landreville continues his appointment, and nothing can be done.
We are surprised also that people have to wait four years for settlement of cases under the unsatisfied judgment fund, not because the lawyers have failed to do their job but because there are no judges available to hear the cases. I think much more has to be done in this field than merely having an opportunity every year or so to say something on this subject when we appoint another judge or two. I think the Government has a responsibility, if they really want to see justice done, to find some way of making all the judges work. It might not be by asking the Chief Justice to report, but some way could be found. Those who do not want to do the job could be retired. We would be better off to pay them a good pension because they are only deadwood, and we would be well rid of them.
We have been able to maintain a very high standard of judges in Ontario. I do not believe there is anyone in Ontario who will not say that justice is on a high level. We are prepared to admit also that there are some who do not want to maintain these high standards, and we would like some method of assuring that the standard is maintained.

I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will pass on to the Minister the desire of some people in this country to have a much more effective way of disciplining judges and maintaining high standards. We probably should have a much better way of appointing judges than for Parliament continually to ask for one or two more. This may not be enough to even meet the backlog, when you take the load off the judges who are sitting now.

speechtext: I rise briefly to say that I listened to some of the interesting and eloquent remarks made by the hon. Member for Timiskaming. I must also bring to the attention of the House that the circumstances he so graphically described do not apply to the judges of British Columbia.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES

I spoke recently, but there was one point I omitted and which I should like to raise now. A few days ago I was interested in reading that a judge who had been found guilty of perjury and sentenced to two years still holds his appointment, although he has not been sitting as a judge. He is still drawing his money. The point I want to raise is that I read in the newspaper that the Minister of Justice said he cannot discharge this judge who has been found guilty of perjury.
I should like to make it clear that, under the circumstances. I believe there is a responsibility on the Minister of Justice to introduce the required motion in the House of Commons. I understand that only the House of Commons can discharge a judge. For the Minister of Justice to say he has no authority to discharge a judge is a statement which I find-I do not know what words to use-picayune, uncourageous and despicable. In other words, it is completely irresponsible. I say it is the responsibility of the Minister of Justice, when a judge has been found guilty of perjury, to introduce the required motion in the House of Commons to discharge him, so he will not sit in judgment on others.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES
speechtext:
Perhaps I may reply to some of the observations that have been made by hon. gentlemen. Perhaps I should hasten to reply, first of all, to the misquotation of the Leader of the Opposition by the hon. Member for Timiskaming. The hon. Member for Timiskaming may have been thinking of a situation in Ontario in which it is not mandatory for magistrates to have legal training. In so far as Superior Court or County Court judges appointed by this Parliament are concerned, it is mandatory

June 25, 1965
Judges Act
that they have legal training. What the Leader of the Opposition was actually saying was that there were circumstances, not infrequently, where a man is appointed to the bench who has not been in active practice in the courts but has conducted the business of a solicitor. Very often the solicitor, who has not been actively practising in the courts, turns out to be a better judge than some of the leading counsel. I think that is the point the right hon. gentleman was making.
The hon. Member also made reference to the distribution of the work load. He observed particularly that during the months of July, August and part of September the court is on vacation. In so far as the question of whether or not there should be such a lengthy vacation, I can only speak for my own Province of Ontario and say that the question has been raised as to whether the vacation is too long, particularly in connection with criminal matters. It has been stated Superior Court judges should be sitting all year round to deal with criminal matters. I believe I am correct in saying that it is not for this Parliament to decree whether the court calendar is run the year round or not; that is a matter of the administration of justice and is for the province. I am sure the hon. gentleman's observations will be noted and given the appropriate consideration.
He made some reference to the statistics I quoted with reference to the case load and referred to the fact that judges at certain levels are entitled to engage in non-judicial activities. I point out to him that High Court judges in Ontario are not entitled to do so, but County Court judges are. County Court judges can take outside work such as to act as arbitrators in labour disputes or as members of local police boards. Supreme Court judges are required to confine themselves to judicial business, except such business as a commissioner under the Inquiries Act to which position they may be appointed by the Governor in Council or the Lieutenant Governor in Council. The case load to which the hon. Member referred has not come about by reason of the fact Supreme Court judges are not attending to their duties. I am sure the Chief Justice would be the first to support me in that remark.
Perhaps the hon. Member does have a valid observation, and it is relevant here because we are considering the position of an additional County Court judge in Ontario, as to whether or not the bench at this level

should engage in non-judicial activities. I point out to him that perhaps there is ground for imposing some limitation on the activities of County Court judges. However, there is recognition of the fact County Court judges perform distinct services within particular communities. I think many people within the labour arbitration field would feel that conciliation would be hampered if it were not possible to get County Court judges to act on arbitration boards.
[DOT] (4:50 pjn.)
Perhaps the hon. Member does not agree with that. I certainly know that that view is held by some people both on the side of labour and of management. Under Ontario legislation County Court judges perform duties as members of local police commissions, and a County Court judge is in some respects almost more an administrative officer within a county than acting in another capacity as a judicial officer. The question is not one without merits on both sides.
With respect to the case load of each judge, I am not in a position to tell the hon. Member that, but with respect to High Court judges the calendar which they are to follow is drawn up by the Chief Justice who, merely from the standpoint of personnel relations, will do his best to equalize the load. But inevitably with justices who are trying cases both in a large metropolitan area like Toronto, and who go out on circuit to small urban or rural communities, there is inequality in the load they have to meet.
I also know it is the practice for the Chief Justice to rotate the work of justices so that they take on the heavy and the light alternately. However, here again there is an inherent inequality, due to the factor of experience and being specialized in certain fields of law. Very often you will find in commercial cases it is desirable to appoint a judge to hear them who has had experience in a large commercial practice.
With respect to County Court judges you have a different situation, in the sense that they are appointed for each county, and in this respect and as a basis of comparison I point out that the County of Dufferin has only about 11 members of the bar while the County of York has I believe over 4,000 members of the bar. There is an essential inequality in the case load, but I would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to Chief County Court Judge Willmott, who was appointed by the previous government, who has attempted to try to distribute judicial talents on a basis of equality so that in
June 25, 1965

those counties where there is a heavy volume of work judges may be brought in from other areas to assist in coping with the volume.

As prompted by the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre, in conclusion I would like to make reference to the remarks of the hon. Member for Vancouver East who appeared to suggest that in the case of a Superior Court Justice in the Province of Quebec the Minister of Justice should have suspended his salary. In the answer which I gave to the House on behalf of the Minister, as recorded at page 2667 of Hansard, I pointed out that in the opinion of the Department of Justice, under the existing provisions of the law it is not possible to suspend remuneration. This leads one in turn to the case of a former Liberal Member of this House, whose name I did not mention but which has now been mentioned. What manner of administration of justice is this, when a judge is convicted of perjury; he appeals immediately- and sometimes appeals take a long time to be heard. He cannot be suspended, under the law, but he can be given leave of absence? Would this not have been a case for granting leave of absence without pay? Just imagine. This is the man who made way for the entry of Mr. Chevrier into Parliament. He went to the bench. And he draws $12,700 as a justice after his conviction. I should like to know what would have happened if the Secretary of State for External Affairs, now removed from politics, was sitting over here and we were in office. Suppose this kind of thing happened. The ferocity of his verbosity would have been justified. We want to know all about this. We are anxious to keep the bench at a high level. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AMOUNTS, EXEMPTIONS, ADMINISTRATION. ETC.
speechtext:
that the House go into Committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952, to incorporate into the Act Schedule A as authorized by the Appropriation Act No. 10, 1964; to allow for further exemptions in property and income; also to provide for certain changes in connection with the administration of the Act.
Motion agreed to and the House went into Committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the Chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AMOUNTS, EXEMPTIONS, ADMINISTRATION. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in accordance with requests from some hon. Members and of the veterans organizations and their officials I propose to take a moment or two to place on the record a brief history and some facts pertaining to the proposed bill.
The War Veterans Allowance Act, now in its 35th year of operation, has been amended 12 times since it was first passed in 1930. These amendments from time to time have broadened the scope of the Act which has become one of the most rewarding Acts contained in the Veterans Charter. Originally known as the "bumt-out" pension, it has been designed to help qualified veterans who, by reason of age or infirmity, are no longer able to make their way in earning their living, and to provide maintenance to widows and orphans of recipients of the allowance. The importance of this Act and the expansion of its benefits since 1930 have been substantial, so that at the end of this last fiscal year 84,213 veterans, widows and orphans were recipients under the War Veterans Allowance Act at a cost of approximately $91,500,000.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Due to the passage of time, only one veteran of the Northwestern Field Force Campaign of 1885 remains on the War Veterans Allowance rolls. For the second year

June 25. 1965

War Veterans Allowance Act in succession, also due to the ravages of time, the number of approved applications from the veterans of World War I has been less than the number of approved applications from veterans of World War II. However, the number of recipients has steadily increased. I feel you will agree it is a source of pleasure to know that our aging veteran population has this security provided for them as they reach the end of the road, either by reason of failing health or age.
In the bill which the Government proposes to bring before you, you will be asked to increase the maximum equity in real property which is allowed a recipient. At the present time, when a recipient enters hospital, a small deduction from his allowance is mandatory under the Act. You will be asked to consider an amendment to abolish any reduction of the allowance when a recipient is hospitalized. This I know will be a welcome amendment for many of our veterans who from time to time enter hospital.
The bill will ask also for amendments granting certain additional discretionary powers to the War Veterans Allowance Board and to improve the administration of the Act.
The substance of the amendments that will be presented in the bill will in effect be a corollary to the increases in the rates and the substantial increases in the ceilings, that were passed by the House last December, these increases being retroactive to September 1, 1964. At that time, I would remind you, the single rate was increased from $84 to $94 per month with the single ceiling being raised, on a monthly basis, from $108 to $133; the married rate at that time was raised from $144 to $161 per month and the married ceiling, on a monthly basis, was raised from $174 to $222; orphans rates were also increased proportionately. Veterans organizations and veterans at large have expressed their satisfaction with those increases which are now enjoyed by approximately 90,000 recipients of the allowances.
It has been the history of this House that improvements in veterans legislation have always received wholehearted support and I am sure that the bill, which stems from this resolution, coupled with the very recent retroactive increases in the rates and ceilings granted last December, will improve the War Veterans Allowance Act which is designed to benefit that portion of our veteran population now advanced in years.

speakeroldname: Hon. Roger Teillet (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUTHORITY OF DIRECTORS, HOME CONSTRUCTION ASSISTANCE, ETC.
AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AUTHORITY OF DIRECTORS, HOME CONSTRUCTION ASSISTANCE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the proposed amendments to the Veterans Land Act will update its provisions to serve the needs of veterans already settled on farms, small holdings and other properties across Canada. They will also make available increased loan amounts for those veterans who wish to be established under the provisions of the Act. Some new concepts leading to improved administration are incorporated as well.
Land settlement legislation for veterans has been a feature of Canadian agriculture for 47 continuous years. Experience under the Soldier Settlement Act after World War I and the Veterans Land Act, after World War II has led to the development of policies, particularly in the field of farm credit, that have had a major impact on Canadian agriculture. Once again, the proposals outlined in the resolution will encompass the application of new techniques which may serve as a pattern for a fast changing Canadian picture.
Realizing the great desire of most veterans to remain under the Veterans Land Act, the farm financial amendments will be brought in line with those of the federal Farm credit Act. Not only is it proposed to increase the maximum loan ceiling for farms to $40,000, but the purposes for advancing assistance will be broadened. Consistent with the pattern of a changing farm community,
where new sources of income are developing largely from the tourist and summer recreation trade and other non-farm sources, financial assistance will be provided to assist a small farmer to develop a small business which may not be related to farming. He may utilize an appropriate part of his farm for tourist or recreational purposes or he may engage in some activity connected with agriculture and forestry development. Evidence indicates that the small farmer must supplement his income from sources other than farming. Admittedly, the land belonging to some small farmers will be absorbed by others, but for the majority of that group who will remain on their farms there is merit in providing an opportunity to take advantage of this new source of off-farm income.
It is anticipated that when the qualifying period is ended as of October 31, 1968, there will exist about 20,000 veterans who will be eligible to take advantage of the Act. Nearly all of this number will apply as small holders, officially classified as part-time farmers. The maximum loan ceiling for this group and for commercial fishermen will be increased to an amount comparable to that available from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It will be possible to have $18,000 to buy a property and repay reestablishment credit for a $2,600 down payment. Veterans who wish to be established after the cut-off date of October 31, 1968, must have been issued a V.L.A. qualification certificate. Those who are qualified in this manner need not have repaid re-establishment credits at that date since it will be possible, if desired, to have this amount incorporated in the subsequent agreement of sale with the Director of the Veterans Land Act.
Among the changes which might be classed as administrative, greater flexibility will result and I would like to mention a few of these proposals. They are, the establishment of a Veterans Land Act revolving fund of $380 million for supplying capital loan expenditures, which will facilitate the lending functions; arrangements to permit the payment by a veteran of interest only during adverse crop periods or sudden periods of long illness; arrangements to reduce the minimum amount of group life insurance to 50 per cent of the. debt and to permit the veteran's spouse to be covered. Then, proposals will be made which will make the veteran responsible for maintaining insurance on his buildings. A further change will widen the purposes for a grant on Dominion, Provincial and Indian land settlements, and en-

In order to motivate qualified veterans to ultilize the provisions of the Act without undue delay after 1968, applications for financial assistance must be made by March 31, 1974. Applications for additional loans from any established veteran will not be accepted after March 31, 1977. By this late date the average age of veterans will be approximately 62 years. As a consequence of inserting these dates in the Act the Director can retain and utilize his trained staff to the best possible advantage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in indicating the business for Monday I may say it had been the intention of the Government to move to go into Committee of Supply on Monday, to give hon. Members an opportunity to express their views on the course which the Government has followed with respect to the Address to the Queen concerning the Legislative Council of Quebec. The representatives of
the parties opposite have indicated that they do not wish to use that opportunity for that purpose. Since the interim supply debate will give an opportunity for any hon. Member who wishes to express his views on that question, the Government has decided to call interim supply on Monday, as soon as we have disposed of the third reading of the Income Tax bill.
With regard to the passage of other legislation yet to be disposed of, perhaps it would be better if I were not too rigid at the moment as to the sequence in which it will be presented.

May I first say with regard to the early part of the Minister's statement that we never accept the situation, here, where the Government suggests to us what we will do in the time at our disposal. If we want to move amendments on interim supply they will be amendments of our choice.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is what I sought to make clear.
Will the bill respecting veterans legislation be available?
It is available now.
Is it the intention of the House Leader to have Wednesday as a target date for adjournment for summer recess?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to be very dogmatic about these things because I find I get into trouble if I indicate a specific date for adjournment; but it was the hope that we could come to adjournment for the recess possibly late on Tuesday night. There are just the veterans legislation, interim supply, supplementaries, and the bill indicated in the Prime Minister's statement having to do with incentives to designated areas, to be dealt with.
With respect to the new incentives to designated areas, is it the intention of the Government to proceed only with the resolution stage? This is a fairly extensive measure.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No; it is the intention to proceed with the bill. I think when hon. Members see it they will find that that is the desirable course, and will commend itself to them.
At six o'clock the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.
